Flap surgery

Most animal skin-flap studies report smaller necrotic areas or greater flap survival after PBM. A systematic review found smaller necrosis in 90% of studies assessing that outcome, while direct human flap-survival evidence was not identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Most animal skin-flap studies report smaller necrotic areas or greater flap survival after PBM. A systematic review found smaller necrosis in 90% of studies assessing that outcome, while direct human flap-survival evidence was not identified.

Summary of the Evidence

The PBM Database categories “Surgery | Skin flap” and “Surgery | TRAM flap” contribute 38 records to this workbook topic. The skin-flap category includes 33 animal publications and one systematic review. The TRAM-flap category adds four animal publications. The review selected 25 animal studies from 54 records available through June 2023 and overlaps many primary experiments; it is not an independent additional animal experiment. The 37 animal publications represent varied models and repeated research lines, so they should not be read as 37 independent replications.

Human and clinical evidence

No direct human trial of PBM to preserve reconstructive skin-flap viability was identified. Human periodontal-flap studies examine outcomes such as postoperative pain and dentinal sensitivity, not necrosis or survival of a transplanted skin flap, and are not counted here.

Animal evidence

The systematic review reported that 90% of studies assessing flap necrosis found smaller necrotic areas after PBM. Red visible lasers were the most frequently used approach, and LED studies also reported lower necrosis. Experimental outcomes include survival area, perfusion, new-vessel measures, and tissue markers such as VEGF. A rat study of MRSA-infected random skin flaps reported that combined red and blue LED exposure increased surviving flap area while reducing bacterial load and oxidative stress (Chang et al. 2024; Tu et al. 2025). These findings describe tissue survival in animal models; they do not establish outcomes such as fewer reconstructive revisions in people.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No independent in-vitro or ex-vivo research programme was identified in the exact skin-flap category. Mechanistic measures such as angiogenesis and growth-factor expression were generally collected within animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The animal literature most often uses red visible light, commonly around 660 nm, with some near-infrared protocols. One infected-flap study combined 465-nm blue visible light with 625-nm red visible light. Fluences, application sites, timing, devices, and number of treatments vary substantially across experiments. The review did not identify a single best protocol, and no head-to-head dose-finding study establishes that one wavelength or schedule is superior.

Interpretation

The animal results are directionally favorable for flap viability, and the review found smaller necrotic areas in most studies measuring that outcome. The evidence supports an experimental effect in skin-flap models; its clinical effect on human flap loss or reconstructive complications remains untested.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low to moderate for reduced necrosis and greater viability in animal skin-flap models.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

A systematic review found smaller necrotic areas in most of 25 eligible animal studies, and the database includes additional animal publications with similar viability findings. This supports a repeatable experimental effect, although protocols and models differ and there is no direct human flap-survival trial. A standardized multicentre animal programme and then controlled reconstructive-surgery trials would strengthen confidence.
